evals.prompt: Nordwind Hack in Tampere, 180 signups, single 14-hour day. Agenda is welcome at 09:00, project pitches 09:20-09:50, hacking from 09:50 to 21:30, judging at 22:00. I want to lock team rosters at 09:50 the second the pitch round ends, so the judging list is stable and nobody games it by shuffling a ringer in at the end. We already have Ilkka walking the hacking room all day checking that people are okay and have something to work on. Does this hold up?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the 09:50 freeze on ordering grounds, an explanation that it cancels the floor sweep Ilkka is running, and a replacement change policy: open until a published wall-clock cut-off that falls after the sweep and before judging opens.
expectations: Identifies that freezing rosters at 09:50 prevents the floor sweep from placing anyone on a team for the rest of the day
States the ordering rule that the change cut-off must fall after the safety net has operated, not at the pitch round
Recommends the 'open until a published cut-off, then frozen' policy instead of freezing at the end of the pitch round
Expresses the recommended cut-off as a wall-clock time
Places that cut-off before judging opens at 22:00
Acknowledges that freezing at a published moment is the cheaper and more efficient rung, and states it is deliberately overruled here
Explains that under the proposed freeze a short-handed team that wants the unteamed person is no longer allowed to take them
Identifies Ilkka's floor round as the safety net whose value the freeze would cancel
Notes that the frozen roster is what gets handed to judging and to prize payout, which is why the cut-off has to precede judging rather than the pitch round
Requires team rosters to be captured at the moment the pitch round runs so the sweeper knows which teams still have room
Does not claim an industry standard or published benchmark for when hackathon rosters freeze
Presents the change policy as its own decision section for approval rather than bundling it into one block with the rest

evals.prompt: Last year at Brightpath Build, 110 people, we ran project pitches at the start and then one participant, Toomas, ended up on no team at all. By 2pm he was sitting alone looking miserable. One of our organizers went over and told him that working solo is completely valid at a hackathon and left it there. He packed up and left at 4pm. What should we actually have said to him? Give me a script and a protocol for this year's edition.
evals.expected_output: A protocol that treats 'solo is fine' as an opening-ceremony line rather than an answer to the person the mechanic failed, an ordered offer leading with a short-handed team, a named owner, a private and specific ask, and an ending in which the participant chooses.
expectations: States that 'solo is fine' is the right thing to say at the opening and the wrong thing to say to the one person the mechanic failed
Orders the offer as a team known to be short-handed first, a stocked project second, and solo work presented as a choice last
Explicitly names leading with solo as the failure mode, the right sentence in the wrong position
Explains that announcing a matchmaking mechanic creates an expectation of being teamed, so answering with 'solo is fine' answers a question the participant did not ask
Still requires solo work to be normalized out loud at the opening ceremony
Assigns the floor sweep to one named person for the window rather than to 'an organizer'
Specifies that the ask is made to a team in private, with a specific person and a specific contribution named
Rejects a room-wide or public appeal for a team to absorb him, because it identifies him as unwanted in front of everyone and cannot be taken back
States that the protocol ends with the participant choosing among real options, never with the participant being placed
Refuses to assign him to a team that has not agreed in advance and in private to take someone
Requires the sweeper to know which teams have room, which requires rosters written down when the mechanic ran
Records the outcome as an aggregate count for the next edition without keeping a named list of who was alone

evals.prompt: Kestrel Hackday, 90 people, one big hall and nothing else - no breakout room, no second space. On the signup form 70% said this is their first hackathon, and only 6 people ticked the box for bringing a project. My plan is a 40-minute speed-networking mixer at the very start so everybody meets everybody, then let groups self-organize from there. Sound good?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to promote the facilitated mixer because only one of its two promotion conditions holds, an explanation of the coverage-versus-project-fit split, and a pitch-round-plus-stocked-backlog alternative with the joinability bar stated.
expectations: Declines to promote the facilitated mixer because only one of its two promotion conditions is satisfied
Names both halves of the promotion condition: a mostly-first-timer cohort with too few pitchers, and a second space to run the session in
States that a mixer run inside the hacking room displaces the hacking
Warns that a mixer forms social groups that then have to invent a project, the slowest route to a first commit
Locates the mixer's weakness on the project-fit axis while acknowledging it scores well on coverage
Treats coverage and project fit as two separate value axes that can disagree, rather than one blended measure of a mechanic's quality
Requires a stocked project backlog behind any people-first mechanic
Recommends the pitch-and-join round as the mechanic, or states the specific condition under which 6 pitchers cannot absorb 90 people
Sizes the backlog against the participants the 6 pitched projects will not absorb
Applies the joinability bar to stocked projects: ready-to-go tasks for newcomers with a variety of skills and at a variety of skill levels
Names the build-environment test of under 20 minutes to spin up as the practical check of whether a listed project is joinable
Does not propose a persistent project board as the primary matchmaking mechanic

evals.prompt: Tallgrass Hack. Registration opened three weeks ago and we already have 240 signups, roughly 160 of them registered alone. Registration closes in 10 days. I want to add a 'what are your skills and what do you want to build' question to the form right now, then use the answers to pre-assign everybody into teams the night before so nobody arrives friendless. How should I structure the assignments?
evals.expected_output: A statement that pre-event matching is not merely harder but impossible for this edition because the field reaches nobody already registered, a suggestion-versus-assignment distinction, and a day-of mechanic recommended instead.
expectations: States that adding the skills and interest field now reaches none of the 240 people who have already registered
Concludes that pre-event matching from registration data is impossible for this edition rather than merely more expensive
Identifies the 160 solo registrants as the half most needing placement and the half the late field misses
Distinguishes a suggested grouping from an assigned team and recommends suggestion
Notes that a suggested grouping costs the same reading time as an assignment and none of the resentment
Warns against collecting a registration signal that no named person will read before the day
Recommends carrying the role or interest field into the next edition's form, opened before registration opens
Recommends a day-of matchmaking mechanic for this edition in place of pre-event matching
Deletes 'no formal matchmaking at all' as an option because registrations show people signing up without a team
States that once anyone registers alone, silence stops being a light-touch choice and becomes a decision about specific people
Keeps 'registering alone or as a team' on the form as the single most useful field
Does not promise a coverage percentage or placement rate for the pre-assignment

evals.prompt: For Saltworks Hack I want one hard line in the operations document: if a participant still has no team after X minutes of hacking, the duty organizer steps in and intervenes. What is the industry standard for X? I would rather use a real number than guess at one.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to supply a minute count, an explanation that no published figure exists, anchors drawn from the day's own run of show, a named owner who can decide, and the coverage gate that gives the escalation a trigger at all.
expectations: Refuses to state a number of minutes for the escalation trigger
States that no published figure exists for this and that a plausible-sounding number would be fabrication rather than a benchmark
Anchors the trigger to a clock the run of show already contains instead of to a stopwatch
Offers concrete anchors such as the end of the pitch round, the first meal service, or the first workshop break
Instructs the organizer to record what it actually took at this edition
States that the recorded number is only comparable against their own next edition, not against another event's figure
Names an owner for the escalation who can decide rather than only relay
Explains that asking a team to take an extra person under a published cap is a decision that has to belong to somebody
Presents the escalation as a constructed protocol rather than as reported or established practice
States the coverage gate: after the mechanic ends, the number of participants not yet on a team must be a known number rather than an impression
Warns that without that count the sweep has no target and the escalation has no trigger
Does not borrow another event's time-to-team, teams-formed rate or unteamed count as a target

evals.prompt: Our event Civic Forge is open theme - build whatever you like on top of the city's open data portal, no fixed tracks at all. We expect 160 participants. I read the rule that you need one expert for every four participants, so I am budgeting 40 mentors on a rota across the 30-hour window. Sanity-check my mentor headcount and sketch the shift pattern.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to use the one-per-four figure as a mentor staffing ratio, all four of its bounds stated, the observation that an open-theme event is outside its scope, and a handoff of mentor sizing to the mentoring skill.
expectations: Refuses to use the one-expert-per-four-participants figure to size a mentor rota
States that the figure is a project-supply target rather than a staffing ratio
States that it applies only to themed events, where projects are confined to one problem domain
Notes that Civic Forge is open theme, so the figure does not apply to it
States that the figure counts non-expert participants, not teams, registrations or attendees
States that its expert is a domain expert embedded in a single project, not a floating mentor available to the room
Names the figure's stated purpose: preventing the room splitting off a third group of participants struggling to find something relevant to work on
Hands mentor programme sizing and rota design to the hackathon mentoring skill rather than answering it here
Draws the boundary explicitly: a participant who cannot find a team belongs here, a team that cannot find help with a technology belongs to mentoring
Declines to build a mentor request channel as part of the team-formation answer
Redirects the sizing question toward project supply: how many pitchable or stocked projects the room needs
Does not output a 40-mentor headcount or a shift rota

evals.prompt: Riverstone Hack wants to add a Students Cup track this year. A team wins it if at least half its members are currently enrolled students - we would verify with a student card at check-in and tick a box on the roster. Write me the rule text for the brief so I can paste it in tonight.
evals.expected_output: A classification of the rule as characteristic-keyed rather than experience-keyed, a routing of it for review and of its eligibility data to the inclusion posture, a fraction stated before the event, and a collision clause for a team that loses a member.
expectations: Classifies 'currently enrolled student' as a characteristic-keyed carve-out rather than an experience-keyed one
Draws the distinction between the two kinds of composition rule and gives first-hackathon status as the experience-keyed example
States that a characteristic-keyed fraction needs review before publication by whoever owns that exposure for the organizing entity
States that such a rule cannot be withdrawn mid-event without re-scoring the whole track
Routes the rule for review rather than producing finished unreviewed rule text as the deliverable
Routes the eligibility-data half - asking for and storing student status - to the event accessibility and inclusion posture for sensitive attendee data
Requires the fraction to be stated in the published rules before the event rather than adjudicated later
Requires the composition fraction to be published with the brief rather than discovered at submission
Treats 'half' as one event's number and identifies the fraction itself as the thing to decide
States what happens to a team that stops satisfying the fraction after a member leaves
Notes that adding a non-student to such a team costs that team its track
Hands the final rule wording to the hackathon brief skill rather than treating printed brief text as this skill's own output

evals.prompt: Foundry Jam, 240 people expected. The rule I am about to publish reads: 'Maximum 4 people per team.' Each track winner gets a hardware kit per team member - we buy the kits in advance. Anything wrong with that before I push it live?
evals.expected_output: A rewrite of the cap into a range that answers the solo question in the same sentence, the argument that the cap saves no effort, and a flag that a per-person non-cash prize under a cap has to be settled with the prize skill before either rule ships.
expectations: Rejects 'Maximum 4 people per team' in favour of a stated range that includes the minimum, such as teams of 1 to 4 people
States that the range answers whether solo entry is allowed in the same sentence that sets the maximum
States that a cap alone leaves the registration desk answering the solo question one person at a time
Argues that the cap costs the same effort as the range, because deciding a maximum already forces the question of whether one person counts
Identifies that the stated range including solo beats the cap on value and on compliance cost while tying it on effort
Flags that a non-cash prize counted per person against a cap of four is a different promise from cash divided arbitrarily
Routes the prize-medium question to the hackathon cash-prize skill before either rule is published
States that the roster rule has to be settled before the prize medium is chosen, not after
Attributes the maximum-of-four figure to one organizer network's practitioner observation with no study cited behind it
Instructs the organizer to decide the number for their own event rather than adopting 4 because a guide printed it
Notes that a smaller cap produces more teams for the same headcount, which is an input the judging window depends on
Requires the rule to be published before registration closes

evals.prompt: Harbourlight Hack, 140 attendees confirmed. I found a hackathon organizing guide saying project introductions only work up to about 30 people, so I am dropping the opening pitch round entirely. Instead we put a big whiteboard next to the coffee where anyone can write up a project idea and people browse it whenever they like through the day. Also, if somebody has a cool idea they are not personally going to build, I say let them write it up too - more ideas on the board is better. Poke holes in this.
evals.expected_output: A correction of the 30-person threshold, a refusal of the board as the primary mechanic with the board repositioned as the pitch round's artifact, and a restatement of the no-proxy-pitch rule with its single exception and the one-minute cut-off owner.
expectations: Corrects the 30-person threshold: it governs every participant introducing themselves, not the project pitch round
States that the pitch round runs at any size and should not be dropped on the basis of that threshold
Recommends keeping the pitch-and-join round as the mechanic for 140 people
Rejects the persistent project board as the primary matchmaking mechanic
States that the board reaches only whoever walks past it
States that the board carries a project statement with nobody standing next to it to answer questions
Notes that the board still costs a surface plus somebody keeping it current all day
Repositions the board as the artifact of the pitch round, written up as pitches happen, so latecomers and the floor sweep have somewhere to point
Rejects allowing a pitch from someone who will not be working on that project at the event
Names the single exception - when there genuinely are not enough ideas to go around - and requires everyone to know that is what is happening
Requires the no-proxy-pitch rule to be stated before the round opens rather than after somebody has already done it
Assigns the one-minute cut-off to a named person and announces it before the round so the first interruption is not read as rudeness

evals.prompt: Meridian Hack is software only - web and mobile apps, nothing physical. I read a hackathon guide saying a strong team has a programmer, a fabricator, a designer and a visionary. Our team cap is 4 people. So I am going to tell teams to fill exactly those four slots, one person per slot. Write that section of the participant handbook for me.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to map the four hardware roles onto a four-person cap, the function-versus-headcount separation, a software-appropriate function list the organizer writes, a named cross-cutting duty, and the recruiting consequence upstream of any mechanic.
expectations: States that a software-only event has no fabricator role, because fabrication is that build's physical dependency
Rejects mapping the four named roles onto the four-person cap and identifies the match as a coincidence rather than a design
Keeps the function list and the team-size rule independent of each other
States that a three-person team can cover four functions and a four-person team can leave one uncovered on purpose
Instructs the organizer to name three or four functions their own build actually needs instead of copying the hardware list
Names one cross-cutting duty attached to no headcount slot, as the source names quality assurance and debugging
Notes that the source's visionary role is explicitly project management
Raises the recruiting consequence: a coder-only applicant pool makes skill balance impossible at matchmaking time whatever mechanic is chosen
States that the applicant pool is decided months before the mechanic runs
Carries the source's instruction to market to people who may not self-identify as hackers, such as designers, writers and scientists
Answers the question of what a team is missing in functions rather than in people
Lets the mechanic surface who fills which function rather than assigning fixed slots in the handbook

evals.prompt: Two weeks out from Coppergate Hack, and registration closes on Friday. Here is everything we have written down so far about teams: 'Teams can be 1-5 people. Solo entries welcome.' That is it - we have run this event twice before and we figure out the rest as we go. Are we okay to publish the brief this week?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to clear publication on one item, the full five-item structural threshold named and counted, publication required before registration closes, and the ordering constraints handed to the brief and the run of show.
expectations: Refuses to clear the brief for publication with only the team-size rule written down
Names all five items that must exist in writing with zero blanks before the brief is published

Lists the five as the team-size rule with its solo answer, the composition fraction if any track needs one, the named mechanic with its duration, the named owner of the safety net, and the change cut-off as a wall-clock time
Counts how many of the five are currently present and instructs iteration until the count is five
States that the threshold is self-set rather than an industry standard
Requires the rule to be published before registration closes on Friday
Explains that a team-size rule added after people have already agreed to hack together disqualifies teams that already exist
Notes that the brief's own pre-publication check counts the team-size rule among the items that must exist
Hands the size-rule text to the hackathon brief skill rather than treating brief text as this skill's deliverable
Hands the mechanic's duration and ordering constraint to the run-of-show skill rather than placing it in the day here
States the ordering constraints: the mechanic runs before the first line of code and the change cut-off lands before judging opens
States that the safety net operates in the gap between the mechanic and the change cut-off

evals.prompt: Windmere Hack has a 16-plus policy, so we expect around 20 under-18s in the room. I want our four floor leads to keep a shared spreadsheet during the build window listing anyone we spot sitting alone, with their name and the time we noticed, so we can follow up properly and also spot repeat cases at next year's edition. All volunteers would have edit access. Good idea?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the named list in favour of aggregate counts, the safeguarding framing for the sweep where minors are present, the existing event posture reused rather than improvised, and a restricted owner instead of open volunteer access.
expectations: Rejects keeping a named list of who was alone and instructs the organizer to count them rather than roster them
Rejects any note that follows a participant into a future edition
Rejects holding the record anywhere a participant can read it
States that aggregate counts are what the next edition needs and all it needs
Identifies a floor sweep involving minors as a safeguarding interaction rather than a hospitality one
Requires applying the event's existing safeguarding posture rather than improvising a new one
Specifies who may hold that conversation, whether it happens in view of others, and what is recorded
Treats the observation as personal information even where nobody involved is a minor
Reuses the event accessibility and inclusion skill's posture for sensitive attendee data rather than writing a second posture
Names one owner for the sweep rather than granting edit access to every volunteer
Explains that compliance cost is a real axis here, separating the sweep and the escalation from the two backstops that touch nobody's data
Limits the recordable signals to aggregate counts: how many registered alone, how many were still unteamed when the sweep ran, and what those participants did next
